group.title: More rare adjectives
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Unlikely to offend anyone, and often rather dull.
examples: The speech was polite but {anodyne}.
wrong: The anodyne remarks shocked and offended the whole audience.

words.meaning: Widely told but probably not true.
examples: The story about the famous apple is probably {apocryphal}.
wrong: The apocryphal story is fully proved by many records.

words.meaning: Showing signs of future success.
examples: The team made an {auspicious} start to the season.
wrong: It was an auspicious start: everything went wrong at once.

words.meaning: Threatening harm or evil.
examples: The dog gave the stranger a {baleful} stare.
wrong: Her baleful smile made the children feel safe and welcome.

words.meaning: Connected with pleasant country life.
examples: They left the city for a {bucolic} life on a farm.
wrong: The bucolic scene showed crowded streets and traffic jams.

words.meaning: So complicated that it is hard to understand.
examples: The tax rules are {byzantine}.
wrong: The byzantine form had one simple question on it.

words.meaning: Only imagined, and impossible in reality.
examples: His dream of free energy proved {chimerical}.
wrong: The chimerical plan was simple and already working well.

words.meaning: Too sweet or too sentimental, so it becomes unpleasant.
examples: The film’s ending was {cloying}.
wrong: The cloying dessert had almost no sugar in it.

words.meaning: Done without a plan, purpose or enthusiasm.
examples: They made {desultory} conversation while waiting.
wrong: His desultory search was careful, planned and thorough.

words.meaning: Slow to act, often causing delay.
examples: The council was criticized for its {dilatory} response.
wrong: Her dilatory reply arrived within five minutes.

words.meaning: Still existing, especially of old documents.
examples: Only two copies of the letter are still {extant}.
wrong: The extant manuscript was lost centuries ago.

words.meaning: Silly and pointless, without seeming to know it.
examples: He made a {fatuous} remark about the weather.
wrong: Her fatuous comment was wise and very helpful.

words.meaning: Happening by lucky chance.
examples: Our meeting at the airport was {fortuitous}.
wrong: The fortuitous meeting had been planned for months.

words.meaning: Fast, energetic and rather wild or out of control.
examples: The last week before the launch was {frenetic}.
wrong: The frenetic afternoon was slow, calm and quiet.

words.meaning: Too much, so it seems insincere, especially of praise.
examples: His {fulsome} praise of the boss embarrassed everyone.
wrong: Her fulsome praise was just one brief, cool word.

words.meaning: Closely related to the subject being discussed.
examples: Her point was not {germane} to the debate.
wrong: The germane fact had nothing to do with the case.

words.meaning: Causing deep public shame.
examples: The champion suffered an {ignominious} defeat.
wrong: His ignominious exit made him a proud national hero.

words.meaning: Never changing and impossible to change.
examples: Some believe the laws of nature are {immutable}.
wrong: The immutable rules change every week.

words.meaning: Having very little money.
examples: As an {impecunious} student, he lived on bread and soup.
wrong: The impecunious family bought a yacht for fun.

words.meaning: Just begun, and not yet fully formed.
examples: Her plans were still {inchoate}.
wrong: The inchoate design was finished down to the last detail.

words.meaning: Impossible to remove or forget.
examples: The trip left an {indelible} memory.
wrong: The indelible ink washed off in seconds.

words.meaning: Harmful to something or working against it.
examples: Constant noise is {inimical} to good work.
wrong: Exercise is inimical to health, so doctors recommend it.

words.meaning: Impossible to avoid or escape.
examples: Change is an {ineluctable} part of life.
wrong: The ineluctable result was easily avoided.

words.meaning: Likely to cause resentment or seem unfair.
examples: It’s {invidious} to praise one child in front of the others.
wrong: Making an invidious choice pleased everybody equally.

words.meaning: Just starting to develop.
examples: The country’s {nascent} film industry is growing fast.
wrong: The nascent company has existed for two hundred years.

words.meaning: Wicked and criminal.
examples: The gang was involved in {nefarious} activities.
wrong: His nefarious deeds earned him a medal for kindness.

words.meaning: Very unpleasant, especially smelling bad.
examples: A {noisome} smell came from the drains.
wrong: The noisome scent of fresh roses filled the room.

words.meaning: Serving no real purpose; not needed.
examples: The final chapter seems {otiose}.
wrong: The otiose sentence was the most essential part of the text.

words.meaning: Expecting to be obeyed at once, without discussion.
examples: He gave a {peremptory} order to leave.
wrong: Her peremptory tone politely invited discussion.

words.meaning: Seeming to warn of something important, or trying too hard to sound serious.
examples: There was a {portentous} silence before the verdict.
wrong: The portentous pause meant nothing and felt light and silly.

words.meaning: Remarkably large or impressive.
examples: She has a {prodigious} memory for names.
wrong: His prodigious talent was tiny and ordinary.

words.meaning: Likely to lead to success; favorable.
examples: It wasn’t a {propitious} time to ask for a raise.
wrong: The storm made it a propitious day for sailing.

words.meaning: Very idealistic but not practical.
examples: His {quixotic} plan was to end hunger alone.
wrong: Her quixotic goal was realistic and easy to reach.

words.meaning: Little known and hard to understand.
examples: The lecture covered {recondite} points of grammar.
wrong: The recondite fact was common knowledge to every child.

words.meaning: So silly that it makes people laugh.
examples: The excuse was {risible}.
wrong: His risible argument was taken very seriously by experts.

words.meaning: Healthy, or pleasant and clean to live in.
examples: They moved to a more {salubrious} part of town.
wrong: The salubrious district was dirty and dangerous.

words.meaning: Seeming right or true, but actually false.
examples: His argument was {specious}.
wrong: The specious claim was completely correct.

words.meaning: Very loud and powerful, of a voice.
examples: The sergeant’s {stentorian} voice filled the yard.
wrong: His stentorian whisper could hardly be heard.

words.meaning: Done secretly so that others do not notice.
examples: She took a {surreptitious} look at her phone.
wrong: His surreptitious wave was seen by the whole room.

words.meaning: Full of twists and turns, or too long and complicated.
examples: We drove up a {tortuous} mountain road.
wrong: The tortuous road ran perfectly straight for miles.
